title: Barbershop 2: Back In Business
full_review:
A mom-and-pop haircutting establishment gets shaved by some big-name competition in "Barbershop 2: Back in Business" (MGM).

Tim Story, who directed the sleeper hit "Barbershop" in 2002, hands over the director's, as well as the barber's, chair to Kevin Rodney Sullivan. The sequel, continues its predecessor's irreverent, politically incorrect brand of humor, finding farce in follicles and laughter in lather.

Ice Cube returns as Calvin Palmer, the pensive proprietor of the titular tonsorial parlor he inherited from his father. A cornerstone of Chicago's South Side community, the storefront hangout is a place where a motley crew of old-timers, young homies and hangers-on gather to chat, chill, play dominoes and even get haircuts. Having steered the shop safely through the financial straights of the earlier film, Calvin has settled comfortably into fatherhood, trying, as best he can, to live up to his own dad's pillar-of-society legacy.

But when "Nappy Cutz," a national chain equipped with state-of-the-art grooming equipment, wide-screen TVs and an indoor basketball court waiting area, sets up shop across the street, threatening to put them out of business, Calvin and his barbershop sextet find themselves singing the blues.

Further complicating matters is Nappy Cutz's oily business rep, Quentin Leroux (Harry Lennix), who entices several other local shopkeepers to sell their properties to large real estate interests -- all in the seductive name of "progress."

Helping Leroux in his efforts is Alderman Brown (Robert Wisdom), a slick-talking political parody whose graft-greased palm gives new meaning to the barbershop phrase "take a little off the top."

Of course, all this plot stuff takes a back seat to the boisterous banter and raucous rhetoric that is the film's raison d'etre. The story line, though weightier than that of the first movie, serves the similar purpose of supplying the film's comic spark.

Familiar faces include token white boy Isaac (Troy Garity), uptight Jimmy (Sean Patrick Thomas), gentle-souled Dinka (Leonard Earl Jones) and sassy Terri (rapper Eve). But the sharpest scissors (and tongue) still belong to Eddie (Cedric the Entertainer), the shock-wigged storefront philosopher who holds court cutting what's on your head while he speaks what's on his mind.

Sound-off topics range from the daffy (biracial celebrities) to the disagreeable (including calling the D.C. Sniper the "Jackie Robinson" of crime because he broke the color barrier of serial killers), to the downright distasteful (Michael Jackson's child molestation allegations). And while some might find the raw repartee off-putting, it is refreshing to see a depiction of an ethnically diverse group not only co-existing peacefully but thoroughly enjoying each other's company.

And though some viewers may wish to split hairs, the film presents a positive image of inner-city life. There are none of the usual ghetto cliches (drug dealers, pimps or gang members), just honest, hard-working people concerned about their families and neighborhood. In doing so, it imparts a strong message about the importance of community in maintaining the fabric of a healthy society.

This point is driven home during a Capraesque speech which Calvin delivers before a city review board, which, apart from some unnecessary coarse expressions, is commendable for its incorporation of Gospel values into its discussion of social justice issues. It also reminds us that in our materialistic world of ubiquitous Starbucks, it is people who make communities, and when family-run businesses are elbowed out by superstore conglomerates, neighborhoods lose not only shops but part of their soul.

"Barbershop 2" is a film with heart as well as hair.

Due to an implied sexual encounter, fleeting drug content, brief violence, and recurring crude language and humor, as well as profanity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
